rationale: B wins because its angles are cleaner, fewer, and more alive to an actual editor: “Duolingo's paid subscribers can now video-call an AI cartoon to practice speaking” is a story, not a taxonomy exercise. A has good rigor, but it pads the deck with overlap, especially “Duolingo puts its new AI feature behind a paywall and its new course out front for free” sitting too close to the markets/paywalled-AI angle. B needs a grounding scrub, but it gives the founder sharper press paths faster.
gaps_in_A: “Data lens (relationships) applied to the business model itself” is consultant fog. The paywall/free angle is useful, but that label makes it sound like the writer got lost in its own framework.

“Behind Duolingo's record user growth: two new bets and a profitable balance sheet” is the weakest kept angle: “balance sheet” overstates the supplied fact, which only says publicly traded and profitable.
A splits the paid-AI business story across “paywall,” “9-minute sessions,” and “markets” angles. They are distinct enough to survive, but not distinct enough to avoid smelling padded.
“same quarter” and “ahead of earnings” are not in the update. Tiny inventions still count; reporters notice the loose screw before they admire the machine.
gaps_in_B: “priciest tier” is not supplied. The update says paid Max subscribers, not where Max sits in Duolingo's pricing ladder.
“what critics say apps lack” invents a more specific educator critique than the update provides. The fact is “gamification as shallow learning,” not “apps lack conversation practice.”
“AI cartoon” is punchy but needs care. The update says character Lily; cartoon is likely true in the real world, but it is still not in the supplied fact set.
“habit machine” is a useful frame, but it leans on interpretation. Keep it only if Duolingo will substantiate habit, retention, or cross-subject engagement beyond DAU growth.
